chapters.title: PRE-SUASION: An Introduction
chapters.sourcePressure: The introduction establishes pre-suasion as the work done before the request, using the infiltration of persuasion trainings, prepared-ground logic, anchoring examples, and Jim the fire-alarm salesperson with an ethical wrinkle.
chapters.coreMove: Shift the planning question from what to ask to what should be made receptive before the ask.
chapters.commonMisread: Pre-suasion means making a smoother pitch or clever first impression.

chapters.title: Privileged Moments
chapters.sourcePressure: The source defines privileged moments as points when people are unusually receptive because the right self-relevant idea is active, including pre-questions about helpful or adventurous identity.
chapters.coreMove: Spot the short window when a question has made the right identity available for the real request.
chapters.commonMisread: Any good timing or emotional mood is a privileged moment.

chapters.title: The Importance of Attention . . . Is Importance
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says attended items gain extra perceived importance at decision time, sitting between privileged moments and focal-as-causal logic.
chapters.coreMove: Notice when attention is silently upgrading one factor from present to important.
chapters.commonMisread: The most noticeable factor is naturally the most important factor.

chapters.title: What's Focal Is Casual
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says channeled attention can make a visible feature feel causal, so what is focal can be mistaken for what explains the outcome.
chapters.coreMove: Separate what is most visible from what is actually causing the result.
chapters.commonMisread: If something keeps appearing in the story, it must be the reason the story happened.

chapters.title: Commanders of Attention 1: The Attractors
chapters.sourcePressure: The source identifies threat, difference, and goal relevance as attractors that seize attention and shape what later persuasion can work with.
chapters.coreMove: Use naturally attention-grabbing cues only when they truthfully belong to the decision.
chapters.commonMisread: Make the message louder, scarier, or weirder so people cannot ignore it.

chapters.title: Commanders of Attention 2: The Magnetizers
chapters.sourcePressure: The source identifies self-relevant, unfinished, and mysterious cues as magnetizers that hold attention long enough for later association and persuasion.
chapters.coreMove: Hold attention by opening a personally relevant or unfinished loop that the later message can legitimately close.
chapters.commonMisread: Create suspense or mystery regardless of whether it serves the choice.

chapters.title: The Primacy of Associations: I Link, Therefore I Think
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says a focal concept can become more important and attractive when linked to favorable meanings already present in the audience.
chapters.coreMove: Attach the target idea to a true favorable association already alive in the audience.
chapters.commonMisread: Any positive vibe near a request will transfer to the request.

chapters.title: Persuasive Geographies: All the Right Places, All the Right Traces
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says messages are shaped by physical and psychological places, and that placement context can reduce resistance before merits are weighed.
chapters.coreMove: Move the message into a setting whose traces make the desired meaning easier to receive.
chapters.commonMisread: Decorate the environment until people feel good.

chapters.title: The Mechanics of Pre-suasion: Causes, Constraints, and Correctives
chapters.sourcePressure: The source explains mechanisms, constraints, and correctives: concepts fire when readied, not only when ready, and pre-suasion has limits rather than magical force.
chapters.coreMove: Test whether a prepared concept is truly relevant, temporary, and correctable before relying on it.
chapters.commonMisread: Priming lets you plant any idea and make it work.

chapters.title: Six Main Roads to Change: Broad Boulevards as Smart Shortcuts
chapters.sourcePressure: The source identifies reciprocity, liking, authority, social proof, scarcity, and consistency as broad influence shortcuts that can be frontloaded.
chapters.coreMove: Choose the one influence principle that honestly fits the choice and make it salient before the request.
chapters.commonMisread: Cycle through six persuasion tricks until one gets compliance.

chapters.title: Unity 1: Being Together
chapters.sourcePressure: The source adds unity as a seventh principle and narrows this route to We relationships based on identity, family, genetic commonality, and place.
chapters.coreMove: Bring a legitimate shared identity to consciousness before asking for cooperation.
chapters.commonMisread: Unity means being likable, warm, or team-spirited.

chapters.title: Unity 2: Acting Together
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says We relationships can also be produced by synchronized or collaborative activity, increasing liking and support through acting together.
chapters.coreMove: Create togetherness through shared action before the request rather than merely naming shared identity.

chapters.title: Ethical Use: A Pre-Pre-Suasive Consideration
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says the first decision is ethical use, warns that profit can outrank ethics, and argues unethical tactics undermine organizational profits in three ways without naming them in the sidecar.
chapters.coreMove: Decide whether the attention plan should be used before deciding how to use it.
chapters.commonMisread: Ethics is a compliance note after the persuasive design is finished.

chapters.title: Post-Suasion: Aftereffects
chapters.sourcePressure: The source says pre-suaders want temporary attention shifts to become durable and that two kinds of procedures can help initially generated changes take root.
chapters.coreMove: Convert a momentary yes into a lasting pattern by designing what happens immediately after attention has done its work.
chapters.commonMisread: Once the person agrees, the influence work is done.
